newsitem.title: CANADA: Manitoba deploys 1,500 soldiers against flood.
newsitem.headline: Manitoba deploys 1,500 soldiers against flood.

text.p: More than 1,500 Canadian soldiers were being deployed on Thursday to battle the swelling Red River, as the provincial metropolis, Winnipeg, scrambled to raise dikes against the approaching flood waters.
Winnipeg's mayor declared a state of emergency late on Wednesday as health officials planned to transfer half the patients from Manitoba's second largest hospital.

"We'll have 1,500 to 1,600 soldiers across southern Manitoba by Friday. We lost three lives so far in this flood. That's three lives too many. We're fighting for people's lives," said Canadian armed forces Major Douglas Martin.
Two boys and a man were presumed drowned so far this week.
The Red River was forecast to flood up to 800 square miles (2,072 sq km), making it the worst flood since the 1860s.
A dike around the Red River Floodway -- built in 1968 to protect Winnipeg's 630,000 residents from flooding -- was raised 4.5 feet (1.5 metres) to divert the flood waters.

The C$63.2 million ($45.4 million), 29-mile long (47-km), 30-foot deep (9 metres) crescent-shaped drainage ditch should protect most of the city's 630,000 residents from flooding, said Manitoba flood liaison engineer Larry Whitney.
"If the dike is breached, there will be flooding in the city. But I don't anticipate the probability of that happening to be very high," he said.
Across southern Manitoba, more than three million sandbags were laid and many flood-prone areas needed more.
"I come home every night and I still haven't got any sandbags and the river keeps getting higher. It's 10 feet from my basement," said south Winnipeg resident Antoine Prud'homme.
More than 17,000 residents of the Red River Valley between the U.S. border and Winnipeg have been ordered out of their homes.

Martin Ruest, one of the evacuees instructed to leave her home in the town of St. Pierre Jolys, said: "The water's down a bit in St. Pierre but everyone's still panicking because the Red River water hasn't come in from the States yet."
"Last year was the third worst flood of the century but it looked like peanuts compared to this one," said Montcalm Rural Municipality official Florent Beaudette.
The Red River should crest in Montcalm, which is halfway between Winnipeg and the U.S. border, by May 2.

"It doesn't matter where you go. The Red's rising, the Lasalle River is flooding, we're sandbagging everywhere in the valley," said Brian Phillips, a spokesman for the grain handling firm Manitoba Pool Elevators.
The St. Boniface Hospital -- Manitoba's second biggest -- across the Red River from downtown Winnipeg, said it would transfer half its 500 patients to other hospitals.
"We're one step beyond planning," said Manitoba Deputy Health Minister Sue Hicks.
The hospital last evacuated patients in the 1950 flood, when 100,000 Winnipeggers were forced from their homes.
